utterances.text: I would leave it there and it would always be at the same place. But nobody else took it. It stayed at the barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But when you left your automatic rifle at the barracks, would you have to sign any papers to that effect?

utterances.speaker: SUAD JUSOVIC
utterances.text: Our rifles would be recorded by the logistics officer who was there. So we had our own internal documents, and they were circulating there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that automatic rifle could in theory then be used by somebody else?

utterances.speaker: SUAD JUSOVIC
utterances.text: Mine wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not yours, because you were a commander?

utterances.speaker: SUAD JUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to move on to another topic now. The Prosecution has asked you about the mujahedin and you replied in a spontaneous way that as far as you knew at the Mehurici camp there were some. And you also mentioned the fact that there might have been some at Bijelo Bucje.

utterances.speaker: SUAD JUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, at Bijelo Bucje. At Bijelo Bucje there were some.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And how did you know that there were some at that place?

utterances.speaker: SUAD JUSOVIC
utterances.text: Because I used to see them there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because you yourself were in the area?

utterances.speaker: SUAD JUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what were they up to there?

utterances.speaker: SUAD JUSOVIC
utterances.text: They were staying in a house there, between six and eight of them. But I don't know what they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were they armed? Did they have any vehicles?

utterances.speaker: SUAD JUSOVIC
utterances.text: They didn't -- I did not see them carrying either weapons or driving around in a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you yourself, you were stationed in that area. You were facing the enemy basically?

utterances.speaker: SUAD JUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And were there trenches there which had been dug or did you have any other static or moving positions Did you have set positions?

utterances.speaker: SUAD JUSOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were trenches and there were places from where we could observe the enemy. Observation posts, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And those mujahedin who were staying at that house, six, seven, or eight, did they stay there for a long time or did they leave or -- first of all, at what distance was that house from where you were?

utterances.speaker: SUAD JUSOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps 200 metres. A kilometre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you never knew what they did there?

utterances.speaker: SUAD JUSOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you saw those people with your own eyes or had you simply been told that there are foreigners a kilometre away, or did you actually see them at such?

utterances.speaker: SUAD JUSOVIC
utterances.text: I saw them myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could you describe their physical appearance, their clothes?

utterances.speaker: SUAD JUSOVIC
utterances.text: They were wearing -- how should I describe this? Like a jacket, which was slightly longer, down below the knee. And they were wearing slippers, and they had long hair and long beards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And did you talk to them?

utterances.speaker: SUAD JUSOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you remind us of the period of time when you yourself were at Bijelo Bucje.

utterances.speaker: SUAD JUSOVIC
utterances.text: I mentioned already when I was there once every fortnight there was a change of shift. And between April and May I was on the front line for about 45 days. I never went anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were there before the change of shift. So you had to be there in January, February, and March.

utterances.speaker: SUAD JUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And my last question: You talked about this rotation or the change of shifts. On the basis of your replies, we have seen that you were holding certain positions along the front lines for a certain period of time, in this case it was 45 days, and then you were meant to go back to barracks, and at that stage you would take leave. Was that the way it was?

utterances.speaker: SUAD JUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, the leave period, how long was it, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: SUAD JUSOVIC
utterances.text: It could last for anything between three, five, or maximum eight days, depending on needs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And after this period of leave, if for example it lasted for a week, you would go back to barracks and what would happen there? You would be sent to another geographical area or would you just go back home and wait for instructions?

utterances.speaker: SUAD JUSOVIC
utterances.text: When we went back to barracks, we would have preparations for three or four days and then we would go back to the front line where we were before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like to give the floor the Prosecution first for any extra questions they might have. Do you wish to ask any questions on any points of clarification?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I think the Prosecution just has two questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. Jusovic, could you tell me, and pardon me for me pronunciation, could you tell me how big was Bijelo Bucje in terms of numbers of houses or buildings? How large was this area?

utterances.speaker: SUAD JUSOVIC
utterances.text: 120 houses perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And could you tell us approximately how many inhabitants, how many people lived there?

utterances.speaker: SUAD JUSOVIC
utterances.text: Around 600.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And in this area, would there also be local civilians living there as well?

utterances.speaker: SUAD JUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have several questions to put to the witness for the sake of clarity.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jusovic, the Presiding Judge asked you where the fighters of your battalion were coming from. On page 33 of the transcript, line 4, when clarifying the makeup and the structure of the 7th Muslim Brigade you explained that, as it says there, within the brigade there were fighters from 68 -- between 68 and 72 municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is that what you said in reply to the questions put to you by my learned friend?

utterances.speaker: SUAD JUSOVIC
utterances.text: I believe it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that it was very difficult for fighters to always gather in order to change shifts on the front lines. You said that some of the members of your battalion lived as far as Nemila in the vicinity of Zenica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD JUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In reply to the questions put to you by the Presiding Judge you also said that you had shifts in the area of responsibility of your battalion on the front lines along Bijelo Bucje and that those shifts would change once a fortnight. Would it be correct, Mr. Jusovic, if I was to say that that was the case all the way up until the month of April, 1993, when your company had to stay there for 45 days?

utterances.speaker: SUAD JUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the other fighters from your battalion in the course of that period of time, that is to say between April -- or as of April could not go back to their duties within their companies and battalions due to the fact that the roads were blocked and communications were cut off between the places where they took leave and the places where they were meant to carry out their combat duties?

utterances.speaker: SUAD JUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that, Mr. Jusovic, at that period of time as a matter of fact and due to an attack carried out by the HVO in the entire valley of Lasva there was a total block of all communications for civilians as well, let alone soldiers between the area of Zenica and Travnik?

utterances.speaker: SUAD JUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If my understanding is correct, that was the main reason why your company was unable to leave the front lines at Bijelo Bucje for almost 45 days. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD JUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your reply to the previous questions you said that in that period of time the 4th Company - and the commander of that company was Enver Adilovic - was in the area of Poculica. Is it correct that that place, Poculica, is not far from Vitez and those fighters as well were not in a position at that particular period of time to get to Travnik?

utterances.speaker: SUAD JUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So basically, the fighters within the 4th Company, as we have heard from the witness Enver Adilovic, were often called Vitez Company because most of them either lived or came from the area of the municipality of Vitez. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD JUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, they went there a few days after the events in Ahmici. And that was after the 16th of April, 1993, when the HVO attacked Ahmici. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD JUSOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Given the composition of the brigade that was from the area of 68 to 72 municipalities, according to your testimony, would it be correct to say, Mr. Jusovic, that many of those municipalities were occupied by the Serbian forces during that period?

utterances.speaker: SUAD JUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And most of those combatants as well as yourself were refugees or displaced persons?

utterances.speaker: SUAD JUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And they were staying in the wider area of the free territory of the 3rd Corps, is that correct, in a vast area?

utterances.speaker: SUAD JUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question from the Presiding Judge you mentioned the combat that you participated in and you mentioned significant losses that you had sustained during that period of time. Would it be correct to say that as part of a manoeuvre unit you participated in fierce fighting throughout the summer of 1993?

utterances.speaker: SUAD JUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And that was the reason for which your unit engaged in combat in Fojnica in the area of Vitez on Igman sustained such significant losses?

utterances.speaker: SUAD JUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Defence counsel for Mr. Kubura.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We have no questions, but on page 46, line 24, in response to your question as to how far the house was in which the mujahedin was staying, the house that he had observed, the witness replied that it was 1.200 metres away, whereas in the transcript it says 200 metres away. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Sir, this completes your testimony. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I would like to thank you for coming to The Hague and for having answered the questions put to you by Mr. Kubura's Defence. On behalf of the Chamber, I wish you a safe return to your country and I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we still have some time we'll be able to deal with certain outstanding issues. First of all, could the Defence inform me of the schedule for the following week, as I haven't received any written submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could we go into private session for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Registrar, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now that we're in open session I'd like to inform the Defence that our decision concerning judicial notice will soon be provided; it was signed today. So you should be informed of it very soon. As far as the witness's documents are concerned, document 6 which was not shown, you are not tendering this into evidence? No. I see. Mr. Registrar, there are some documents that are on stand-by; perhaps you could give them definitive exhibit numbers now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. These documents were in fact marked for identification and in accordance with General Hadzihasanovic's -- the Defence for General Hadzihasanovic's request, they will now be given definitive exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'd like to inform the Prosecution of the fact that these were documents that weren't translated. I wanted to ask the Prosecution whether there were any objections and you said that there weren't any objections. Is that correct, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not exactly sure of what documents we're talking about in the absence either copies of the documents or being given the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you show the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution has no objection to the documents on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, could we have the numbers, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will say the numbers in English to make it easier for the court reporter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as that is concerned, Mr. Registrar, before you continue I have noted that sometimes the court reporters changed. And when a new court reporter appears, the names of individuals and places cause certain problems. Could the registrar perhaps provide the new court reporters with a list of names and a list of place names to make sure that the transcript reflects what is said and it won't make it necessary for the Defence to rise to point out errors that are made. It would be good for the court reporters to have a list of place names to the left or to the right so they can immediately enter the names and place names into the transcript. This is something that should have been done years ago. Please proceed now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'll deal with this list of documents and I'll provide the documents with a list of final exhibit numbers. I will do that in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I just wanted to mention the fact that the Defence's offensive when filing these documents through a motion was to avoid what we are now trying to do. This was the procedure followed in the course of the Prosecution case. They filed a list. The Chamber just took note of the list, that is to say they took note of the fact that the ID was being replaced for all these documents. Perhaps we can deal with this in the same matter in order to save time, although we have a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, how many documents do we have there, how many numbers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will follow Mr. Bourgon's suggestion. Mr. Registrar, the Trial Chamber notes that the numbers on the documents marked for identification will now become final exhibit numbers. Could you just mention that this will be done in accordance with the decision that has just been rendered.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll proceed as the Chamber has stated. However the registry has noted that two documents, two references, have already been admitted DH414 and 1936, DH 1936 [In English]... Evidence prior to the request of the Defence of General Hadzihasanovic. [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. As we have some time left, are there any other issues that either of the parties would like to raise? Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would just like to inform the Trial Chamber of the following technical issue. Since we have now started with the Defence case for the second accused we believe, Mr. President, that the only party that has the right to re-examine the witness is Defence counsel for the accused who is presenting his case because as Defence counsel for General Hadzihasanovic we don't have the right to re-examine. This would safeguard the rights of everyone concerned. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When a witness is called by the second accused, we'll have the examination-in-chief, followed by the

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: the Prosecution. When the time for re-examination comes, it's only the party that has called the witness that can re-examine the witness. The Defence team for the other accused does not have the right to re-examine the witness. This would not be fair for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but so far when your witnesses testified, there was the examination-in-chief, the Prosecution's cross-examination, additional questions. And then Brigadier Kubura's Defence counsel asked additional questions, not always but occasionally. And after the Judge's questions everyone had the right to ask new questions, additional questions. This is how we have proceeded so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly, Mr. President. After the Chamber's questions, naturally all the parties have the right to ask additional questions. But in order to avoid any problems in the future, this is why I raise the issue. If the Defence counsel for Mr. Kubura had the opportunity of asking questions, had the opportunity of re-examining the witness, well this isn't something I have noticed so far. But I now see that on two occasions we have been given the possibility of re-examining the witness, whereas that should not really be done, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but the rules don't specify anything in particular. As far as this legal issue is concerned, what is the Prosecution's position?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, we had noticed of course during the course of the Hadzihasanovic case that the Chamber was allowing the Kubura Defence to re-examine the witnesses as well. Certainly the general practice of the Tribunal is that the party who is calling the witness is entitled to re-examine the witness following the cross-examination, and the other parties or other co-accused are not generally entitled to have a second go following their cross-examination. I will simply leave it at that. It is entirely within the Trial Chamber's discretion to control how the proceedings are followed. But I do believe my learned colleague is correct in the sense that the Rules as written, I believe, only allow or only specifically allow for the party calling the witness to re-examine following the cross-examination. And as Your Honours has pointed out, it's a different situation following any questions that the Trial Chamber may have for a witness. I think in those circumstances, all the parties should be given an opportunity to ask further questions. But the general procedure seems to be in and the trial practice here is that the party calling the witness conducts a direct examination, the co-accused would then be entitled to cross-examine, the Prosecution would cross-examine, and then the party who called the witness would be entitled to re-examine, but the co-accused would not be entitled to have a second cross-examination. I think that that is what my learned colleague Mr. Bourgon is referring to. But I simply leave it up to the Trial Chamber in terms of to how to control the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the other Defence team? I can see that Mr. Dixon is looking at the Rules. Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have taken the opportunity to look at Rule 85 (B) which, as Your Honour indicated, does not make it clear which parties can or cannot examine in-chief, cross-examine, and re-examine. The Rule simply says: "Examination-in-chief, cross-examination, and re-examination shall be allowed in each case." And in our submission, the practice has been for the other counsel for the other defendant to have an opportunity to re-examine. That certainly has been the case all along. And we don't see any reason why that need change now, that the Defence for Mr. Kubura is presenting their case. It is entirely for the Trial Chamber to decide how to control the examination of witnesses. The Rules do not specify exactly how that should be done, and it's in our submission for the Trial Chamber to -- in its discretion for Your Honours to determine how best that should occur, and that had worked effectively up until now. And in our submission, we don't see a reason why that should change for our case. So we would have no objection for the Defence team for Hadzihasanovic also asking questions in re-examination in line with the practice up to now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I just have one question for Mr. Bourgon. Allowing you to ask an additional question, how would this cause you prejudice? You're not obliged to put such a question. If you ask a question, that's means it's in your interest. Could you explain that to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the situation is quite the reverse. We don't want any advantages that we don't have the right to. If the Chamber gives us the opportunity to proceed in this manner, it will be our pleasure to do so, but we believe that it's important for the procedure followed to be fair and the time that is allocated for each witness is also an important matter. So we are just emphasising this fact. On a number of occasions we have heard the Prosecution use the phrase "out of an abundance of precaution," so we're just emphasising this fact. But naturally, if the Chamber gives us the possibility of re-examining, we'll take advantage of the fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kubura's Defence team took advantage of this possibility but in a moderate manner and I'm sure that you will do the same. Are there any other issues that you would like to raise? The Prosecution? No matters to raise? Mr. Kubura's Defence team? No issues to raise? In that case, we will now adjourn and I will see you at the hearing on Monday at 2.15 p.m. Thank you.
